supplementary_info.identification_information: From Madge (2020): 38 cm; c. 125 g. A rather large, dark purplish-blue and chestnut jay with forehead and loral feathering somewhat stiffened, crown feathers very slightly elongated (can be inconspicuously erected), tail relatively longer than that of G. glandarius and somewhat graduated at tip, bill rather stout; in shade of forest overall appearance of a very dark bird, with contrasting pale bill and with narrow white trailing edge on innermost secondaries and tail. Has nasal tuft, forehead, loral region, chin and throat black, throat with short white streaks; remainder of head, neck, uppermost mantle and breast dark purplish-blue, lower breast gradually merging into rufous-chestnut, washed with mauve, of remainder of body plumage (with wear, chestnut colour prevalent as purplish feather fringes abraded); tail dark purplish-blue, black subterminal band and white tip; upperwing dark purplish blue, wing-coverts and secondaries finely barred black, tertials unbarred but with prominent white tips; iris dark violet-blue; bill clear pale yellowish, greener base; legs dark grey. Sexes similar. Juvenile is much drabber than adult, with purplish areas of plumage dull brownish or dark greyish, and chestnut areas dull brown, lacks white tips on tertials and tail. Sounds: Most frequent call a harsh, grating "kraah", readily given in alarm by flushed birds, or when mobbing predators; can be uttered at variety of pitches. High-pitched mewing call presumed to be a contact call, as frequently heard from foraging birds. Screech call seems to be given only during display. May call repeatedly from tops of tall trees for up to 3 minutes, speeding up in frequency towards end and ceasing abruptly.

documentation.range: Endemic to the islands of Amami and Kakeromajima, of the Ryukyu Islands, Japan (Brazil 1991, BirdLife International 2001, eBird 2024). The species was reportedly common in the central mountains of Tokunoshima in the 1920s (Kuroda 1925 in BirdLife International 2001), but the record was never confirmed, and the species is no longer present on the island (K. Sugimura in litt. 2001 in BirdLife International 2001). The records from Tokunoshima were either erroneous or the species has become extinct on the island (Ishida et al. 1990b in BirdLife International 2001, Brazil 1991, Madge and Burn 1993).
documentation.population: This species was considered common on Amami and Kakeromajima in the 1970s (Bruce 1979), with the population estimated at c. 5,800 individuals (Nishida 1974, in Brazil 1991). However, the population very likely declined below this estimate by the early 2000s (BirdLife International 2001, Madge 2020) due to the proliferation of Urva auropunctata (Small Indian Mongoose) introduced on Amami in 1979 (Sugimura et al. 2002, 2003, 2013, Ishida et al. 2015). The monitoring of wildlife populations in central Amami estimate that the density of this species decreased from 1985-1986 (1.2 individuals per plot) to a low point in 2000 (0.35 individuals per plot), before increasing again until 2009-2010 (0.51 individuals per plot) after eradication of U. auropunctata began in 2000 (Sugimura et al. 2013). The population is showing continuing signs of improvement (K. Ishida in litt. 2016), and is therefore expected to have continued this upwards trajectory considering the widescale success of the control program on Amami (Kanda 2023). However, the exact population size is uncertain, and the range and population are still considered to be small (Ishida et al. 2015). Therefore, the species is estimated to have a population size of 5,000-9,999 individuals and 4,000-8,000 mature individuals.
documentation.habitats: Widespread within its geographically restricted range, preferring subtropical evergreen broadleaf forests, as well as coniferous, deciduous, and mixed woodlands, throughout the lowlands and mountains (Brazil 1991, Madge 2020). The species may occur in small parties, or in groups of up to 100 birds, roaming through forest and edge habitats, including small shady woodlands, plantations, and villages (Brazil 1991, Madge 2020). The species' is omnivorous, feeding on a variety of invertebrates, as well as seeds and berries (Madge 2020), but it appears to be particularly dependent on acorn production, which influences the timing and success of breeding (Ishida et al. 2015). The species may also feed in agricultural fields if preferred food sources are unavailable (Y. Kominami in litt. 2007).
documentation.threats:
The most significant threat to this species is predation from introduced predators, chiefly U. auropunctata (Small Indian Mongoose) which caused rapid declines in the population during the 1990s (Sugimura et al. 2002, 2003, 2013; Ishida et al. 2015). However, following full-scale control programmes, U. auropunctata numbers have declined to the point they are now almost eradicated on Amami (Kanda 2023, Amami Wildlife Conservation Centre n.d.) and the population of this species has show signs of recovery as a result (Sugimura et al. 2013). Regardless, the species may still be threatened from predation by feral cats and dogs (Shionosaki et al. 2015, 2016) and Corvus macrorhynchos (Ueta and Yamaguchi 1995 in BirdLife International 2001). However, there has been no research into the impacts of C. macrorhynchos and scat analysis of feral cats on Amami found G. lidthi remains in only one of 102 samples (Shionosaki et al. 2016).

The impacts of logging have also decreased over recent decades (Sugimura et al. 2003, Madge 2020) and the species is likely to be tolerant to the small levels of continuing forest loss (Global Forest Watch 2024) due to its tolerance of secondary and modified habitats (BirdLife International 2001, Sugimura et al. 2003, Madge 2020). The species does show some population level responses to the level of acorn production within a season (Ishida et al. 2015), and so any disturbances that target this particular resource is likely to impact the species.

Finally, twelve out of 30 adult birds were found to be positive for avian malaria parasites from surveys conducted 2009-2011, though in comparison to other species in the area, prevalence in this species is thought to be low (Ishida et al. 2015).

The species was previously threatened by the cage bird and feather trades, but these threats are no longer present as the species is protected by law as a National Monument (BirdLife International 2001, Madge 2020).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions Underway
It is legally protected in Japan as a National Monument. A large portion of forest on Amami is protected under a World Heritage Area (UNEP-WCMC and IUCN 2024). Urva auropunctata (Small Indian Mongoose) has been controlled by the Japanese Ministry of the Environment to the point they are almost completely eradicated (Kanda 2023, Amami Wildlife Conservation Center n.d.), and the population has been recovering as a result (Sugimura et al. 2013). The increase in numbers of Corvus macrorhynchos on Amami has been halted by improvements in refuse management (K. Ishida in litt. 2012). There are captive populations at Ueno Zoo and Hirakawa Zoo (Ishida et al. 2015).

Conservation Actions Proposed
Carry out surveys to obtain an up-to-date population estimate, and monitor across key sites to confirm the population trajectory. Provide nest-boxes in areas where there is a shortage of suitable natural nesting sites, which can also provide protection against nest predation (BirdLife International 2001). Further research is required on the impact of feral cats and dogs on the population and the invertebrate community in nests to understand the impacts of invasive parasites and the prevalence of avian malaria (Ishida et al. 2015). Continue to study and monitor the relationship between the population and acorn production, and protect key resources/resource areas where necessary. Continue control of invasive predators on Amami.
documentation.use_trade: The species was historically heavily exploited through the cage bird trade in Japan during the 17th and 19th century, but it was hugely popular internationally for the feather trade between 1909 and 1928, with more than 8,000 killed and exported to Europe and America (Kuroda 1925, Higuchi et al. 1986 in BirdLife International 2001). However, reports suggest that most of this exploitation occurred in the years immediately after 1909, and that by 1917, the population had recovered (Horii 1918 in BirdLife International). The species is now recognised by law as a Japanese National Monument, and is no longer subject to such exploitation (Madge 2020).
documentation.rationale: This species underwent at least two severe population reductions during the 20th century, first from the feather trade and then again due to invasive species. However, the species is now protected as a Japanese National Monument and the recent full-scale eradication of the introduced small Indian mongoose (Urva auropunctata) has led to the gradual recovery of the species' population. There is no evidence to suggest that the population is declining, and the species is consequently listed as Least Concern.
documentation.trend_justification:
This species declined during the 1990s as a result of predation from Urva auropunctata (Small Indian Mongoose) introduced to Amami in 1979 (Sugimura et al. 2002, 2003, 2013, Ishida et al. 2015). However, the population has shown positive signs of recovery after the full-scale eradication of U. auropunctata began in 2000 (Sugimura et al. 2013). The estimated abundance of the population in central Amami has increased from 0.35 individuals per plot in 2001-2002 to 0.51 in 2009-2010 (Sugimura et al. 2013). Control of U. auropunctata on Amami has been sufficiently successful that no mongoose has been captured since 2018, with the current goal to have eradication on the island confirmed by the end of the fiscal year 2025 (Amami Wildlife Conservation Centre n.d.). There is no precise information on the population trajectory since the surveys in 2009-2010, although the population is thought to be gradually increasing in the north of its range, and may be fluctuating in small numbers elsewhere, with no indication that it is decreasing (K. Ishida in litt. 2016). Additionally, the species is expected to be benefiting from the gradual recovery of the Amami forests (Madge 2020) due to logging currently only being economically feasible with government subsidies (Sugimura et al. 2003), and the legal protection of a large portion of Amami forests as part of a World Heritage Area (UNEP-WCMC and IUCN 2024). The current rate of forest loss within the species’ range is c. 1.5% (maximum) over the past three generations (Global Forest Watch 2024, based on data from Hansen et al. [2013] and methods disclosed therein), which is unlikely to have population level impacts considering the species utilises secondary growth, young forest, and plantations (BirdLife International 2001, Sugimura et al. 2003, Madge 2020).

The population may therefore be increasing, in line with several other endemic native species following control of U. auropunctata (Sugimura et al. 2013, Watari et al. 2013, Mizuta et al. 2016, Yagihashi et al. 2021). However, given there has been no recent quantification of the population or its trend, and the continuing and poorly understood impact of predation from feral cats/dogs (Shionosaki et al. 2015, 2016), and Corvus macrorhynchos (Ueta and Yamgushi 1995 in BirdLife International 2001, Madge 2020), the population trend is precautionarily inferred to be stable.
